phonemes.desc: Voiceless dental fricative [θ], the runic thorn that begins many Norse names of power.
Long [uː] plus voiced dental fricative [ð], the name's stressed core meaning "strength, power".
Final [r], the nominative ending of a feminine strong noun.

pronunciation.approximation: 'THROOTH-r' — the first syllable is long and stressed, with the 'th' of 'thin' and a long 'oo' sound; the final 'r' is lightly pronounced.

kin.label: Old Norse

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: From Proto-Germanic *þrūþiz, "strength"; cognate with Old English þrýð

kin.label: Modern Icelandic

pronunciation.note: Þrúðr is Tier 1 because the Old Norse form preserves the distinctive þ (thorn), the long ú, and the ð — all features the ASCII form thrudr loses.

domains.title: Strength
domains.subtitle: Valkyrie and Daughter of Thor
domains.lead: Þrúðr is the very idea of strength made into a goddess. Her name means "power" or "force," and in the Norse sources she is both the daughter of Þórr and Sif and one of the Valkyries who serve in Valhǫll. She embodies the inheritance of the thunder-god — not merely muscle, but the indomitable will that does not break.

cards.name: Daughter of Thor
cards.desc: Skáldskaparmál names Þrúðr among the children of Þórr — the inheritors of storm and strength.

cards.name: Valkyrie
cards.desc: She is counted among the Valkyries in Grímnismál's roster, one of the choosers of the slain who serve in Óðinn's hall.

cards.name: Strength Itself
cards.desc: Her name is a common noun for might; she is the abstraction of force raised to divine personhood.

cards.name: The Karlevi Stone
cards.desc: A runestone on Öland calls a dead chieftain a "thane of Þrúðr" — her name carved on a Viking-Age grave.

mythology.lead: Þrúðr's mythology is sparse but charged: every mention of her name is a mention of power — in a god-list, in a valkyrie-roster, in one full comic tale, and cut in runes at the head of a chieftain's grave.

myths.title: The Daughter in the Catalogue
myths.text: In the Prose Edda, Snorri's chapter on kennings tells the skalds how to name Þórr: son of Óðinn and Jǫrð, husband of Sif — and, in a single catalogue line, faðir Magni ok Móða ok Þrúðar, “father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr” (Skáldskaparmál 4). That line is her whole dossier in the family mythology: no story tells of her childhood, no poem gives her a deed among the gods. Later tradition names Sif as her mother, and the pairing is natural — Sif's hair of gold is the most famous description of female beauty in the Eddas — but the sources themselves are silent on the point. What they insist on is the name: Þrúðr, “strength,” is the only one of Þórr's children whose name is the abstraction of his own domain, as if the thunder-god's defining quality had been given a daughter and sent into the world wearing it.

myths.title: Among the Choosers of the Slain
myths.text: The Poetic Edda lists her again among the Valkyries. In Grímnismál, Óðinn — racked between two fires in the hall of King Geirrǫðr — names the maidens who serve the warriors of Valhǫll: “Hrist and Mist I would have bear me the horn; Skeggjǫld and Skǫgul; Hildr and Þrúðr; Hlǫkk and Herfjǫtur; Gunnr and Gǫndul” (Grímnismál 36). The þulur, the mnemonic name-lists of the manuscripts, count Þrúðr among the Valkyries too. Her placement is exact: like her brothers Magni and Móði, who survive Ragnarǫk to inherit the hammer, she carries her father's might into Óðinn's service — the storm's daughter posted at the gates where the brave are chosen, strength itself keeping the roster of the slain. The two attestations, family list and battle roster, never meet in the corpus; the reader is left to hold both at once.

myths.title: The Suitor Who Talked Till Dawn
myths.text: The one full story the Eddas give her is a comedy of delay. While Þórr was away in the east, the dwarf Alvíss — “All-Wise” — came to Ásgarðr to claim the bride who had been promised him: Þórr's daughter. The prose headnote of Alvíssmál says the gods had pledged her, and Þórr, discovering the betrothal, chose not brute force but interrogation. He received the dwarf courteously and questioned him through the night: what is the earth, the sky, the moon, the sea called among gods, giants, elves, dwarfs, and men? Alvíss knew every synonym — a catalogue of the world's names in six tongues fills the poem — but the knowledge was the trap. When dawn broke and sunlight struck the threshold, the dwarf turned to stone where he stood. Þrúðr never appears and never speaks; her rescue is performed entirely by her father's patience and the sunrise — the myth's quiet joke that the strongest of the gods saves his daughter by simply out-talking a specialist.

myths.title: A Thane of Strength
myths.text: On the Swedish island of Öland stands the Karlevi runestone — raised about 1000 CE for a dead chieftain, its carved dróttkvætt stanza among the finest poetry set in stone in Scandinavia — and the stanza closes with a kenning that names her: the buried man is Þrúðar þegn, “a thane of Þrúðr,” a warrior in the sworn service of Strength (Öl 1). The stone is the one material witness the goddess has: no image, no temple, but her word cut in runes at the head of an aristocrat's grave, where a Christian cross stands beside the old name. The kenning was available to any Viking-Age poet — to be Þrúðr's thane was a ready-made boast — but its choice here shows the name doing live work: to die well was to be enrolled in her household, and the inscription enrolls its chieftain forever, the servant of strength outlasting the flesh that served it.

lore.syncretism: Þrúðr has no foreign cult, but her type — the divine daughter who personifies an abstract quality inherited from her father — is common. Greek Bia and Kratos are the personified forces of Zeús; Roman Virtus is the manly courage that attends Mars. Within Norse mythology she is paired with her brothers Magni and Móði, the sons of Þórr who survive Ragnarǫk and inherit his hammer. Þrúðr is the feminine bearer of that same strength, present both in the divine family and on the battlefield.
lore.culturalLegacy: Þrúðr survives in the modern Icelandic given name Þrúður and in popular retellings of Norse myth, where she is often cast as a warrior maiden or Valkyrie. In Marvel Comics and related media, a version of her appears as Thor's daughter, drawing on the Eddic hint. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice sometimes invokes her for physical strength, endurance, and the will to persist. Restoring Þrúðr preserves the thorn, long vowel, and eth that make her name a visible claim of Norse force.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Þrúðr is strength with a face. In a culture that valued physical courage above almost every other virtue, her name was a compliment and a boast: to be Þrúðr's servant was to be unbreakable. She asks us to consider what strength is for — whether it serves the storm, the battle, or the long endurance that outlasts both.

As a Valkyrie and a daughter, she stands at the intersection of family inheritance and chosen service. She did not choose her father, but she chooses the slain. That double belonging is the human condition: we inherit our bodies, but we decide what to do with them.

lore.archaeology: Þrúðr is primarily a textual figure, but her name appears materially on the Karlevi runestone (Öl 1) on Öland, Sweden, c. 1000 CE. No image or temple can be securely identified with her. Her wider presence is in the Eddic manuscripts and the skaldic poetry that praised dead warriors as her servants.
